sense: promise that something will be so; answer for

evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.3: praestābō sūmptum nusquam melius posse pōnī
Cic. Fam. 1.4.3: Ego tibi ā vī … praestāre nihil possum
terms.comment: To make oneself answerable for something (Lewis & Short): with an object, damnum praestāre, to make good a loss; with an accusative and infinitive, to guarantee that something is or will be so. Its commoner senses are to excel (praestat, it is better) and to supply or show (officium praestāre, to do one’s duty).

evidence: Plaut. Capt. 4.2.118 (old numbering): Spondēn’ tū istud? — Spondeō. (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The solemn pledge of a Roman contract (see promise); to stand surety for someone, prō aliquō spondēre (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: praestābō sūmptum nusquam melius posse pōnī
phrases.english: I guarantee the money could not be better spent anywhere

phrases.latin: Ego tibi ā vī, hāc praesertim imbēcillitāte magistrātuum, praestāre nihil possum
phrases.english: Against violence, especially with the magistrates as weak as they are, I can guarantee you nothing

phrases.latin: quis potest praestāre semper sapientem beātum fore, cum vel in omnibus hīs ūnō tempore esse possit?
phrases.english: who can guarantee that the wise man will always be happy, when he may meet all these at one and the same time?

sources: Lewis & Short: praesto · Lewis & Short: spondeo
Cicero’s letter to Lentulus and the Tusculans checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (11 November 2026); the letter to Quintus is quoted as in the record for spend (money).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
